passages.t: ‘I will exalt You, my God and King’: an alphabet of praise
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “A Psalm of praise. Of David” (verse 1). Then the singer makes a promise. “I will exalt You, my God and King; I will bless Your name forever and ever” (verse 1). “Every day I will bless You” (verse 2).

“Great is the LORD and greatly to be praised; His greatness is unsearchable” (verse 3). No one can measure it.

Praise passes down the generations. “One generation will commend Your works to the next, and will proclaim Your mighty acts” (verse 4). The singer will think on God's wonders (verse 5). Others “will extol the fame of Your abundant goodness and sing joyfully of Your righteousness” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
This is the only psalm whose heading calls it ‘A Psalm of praise’. The Hebrew word, tehillah, is the singular of Tehillim, ‘praises’, the Hebrew name of the whole book. The book page explains the name.

Psalm 145 is an acrostic. The book page explains acrostics. Here each verse begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, from aleph to taw.

But one letter is missing in the traditional Hebrew text. After verse 13, which begins with mem, the next verse should begin with nun. In the traditional Hebrew there is no such line; verse 14 begins with the letter after nun. A line beginning with nun is found in the great Psalms Scroll from Cave 11 at Qumran, among the Dead Sea Scrolls, in some copies of the Greek Old Testament, in the Syriac translation, and in one medieval Hebrew manuscript. The BSB includes it as the second half of verse 13: “The LORD is faithful in all His words and kind in all His actions” (verse 13). Some scholars think the line was lost very early in copying. Others think it was added later to fill the gap. Both views are held, and no teaching of the psalm depends on it.

The book page says that Psalm 145 is part of Jewish morning prayer every day.
passages.later:
Paul gives praise to God as King: “Now to the King eternal, immortal, and invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen” (1 Timothy 1:17).

Verse 4 is the plan God gave Israel from the start: parents telling their children what God has done. Psalm 78 says the same at length.
passages.asks:
‘Every day I will bless You.’ Praise in this psalm is not a mood that comes and goes. It is a daily practice.

And verse 4 asks about the next generation. Who will hear from you what God has done? Children, grandchildren, younger believers, a friend new to faith: one generation commends God's works to the next.

passages.t: ‘The LORD is gracious and compassionate’, and an everlasting kingdom
passages.happening:
Now the centre of the psalm. “The LORD is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and abounding in loving devotion” (verse 8). “The LORD is good to all; His compassion rests on all He has made” (verse 9).

All that God has made will thank him, and his faithful people will bless him (verse 10). They will speak of his kingdom and his might (verse 11), “to make known to men Your mighty acts and the glorious splendor of Your kingdom” (verse 12). “Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and Your dominion endures through all generations” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Verse 8 is not new. It is the description God gave of himself to Moses on Mount Sinai: “The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). This line echoes through the Old Testament, in the prophets and in the Psalms (Psalm 103:8 and 111:4 among them). It was Israel's creed about who God is.

Verse 9 widens it. God's compassion rests on ‘all He has made’. Not only Israel, not only people, but every creature.

The word ‘kingdom’ comes four times in verses 11 to 13. Earthly kingdoms rise and fall. The psalm has seen Israel's own kings fail. God's kingdom lasts through every generation.
passages.later:
The prophets repeat verse 8. Joel calls the people to return to God, “For He is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion” (Joel 2:13). Jonah used the same words when he complained that God was too kind to Nineveh (Jonah 4:2).

Jesus began his preaching with the news that the kingdom of God had come near. In Revelation loud voices cry, “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, and He will reign forever and ever” (Revelation 11:15).
passages.asks:
What do you believe God is like? Many people picture him as quick to anger and slow to forgive. Verse 8 says the opposite, and it is how God described himself.

And verse 9 asks you to look at the world through God's eyes. His compassion rests on all he has made. Whom have you left out of yours?

passages.t: ‘The LORD is near to all who call on Him’
passages.happening:
The last part shows what this King does. “The LORD upholds all who fall and lifts up all who are bowed down” (verse 14). “The eyes of all look to You, and You give them their food in season” (verse 15). “You open Your hand and satisfy the desire of every living thing” (verse 16).

“The LORD is righteous in all His ways and kind in all His deeds” (verse 17). “The LORD is near to all who call on Him, to all who call out to Him in truth” (verse 18). He hears the cry of those who fear him and saves them (verse 19). “The LORD preserves all who love Him, but all the wicked He will destroy” (verse 20).

The psalm ends where it began, with praise, now from everyone. “My mouth will declare the praise of the LORD; let every creature bless His holy name forever and ever” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
Kings in the ancient world were expected to protect the weak and feed the hungry. Few did. Psalm 145 says the LORD does what the best king should do, and more. He lifts those bent over by their load. He feeds every creature at the right time.

‘Food in season’ (verse 15) meant rain and harvest coming when they should, in a land that depended on both.

Notice the word ‘all’. It comes again and again in this psalm: all who fall, all who are bowed down, the eyes of all, every living thing, all who call on him. The singer's praise is as wide as God's care.

Verse 20 is a reminder that God's goodness is not soft on evil. Those who love him are kept; the wicked do not last.
passages.later:
Jesus said, “Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). He pointed to the birds and said, “your heavenly Father feeds them” (Matthew 6:26).

Paul quotes the prophet Joel: “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:13). James writes, “Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you” (James 4:8).
passages.asks:
Are you bowed down? Verse 14 is for you: the LORD lifts up all who are bowed down. Are you far from God? Verse 18 says he is near to all who call on him in truth. You do not need fine words. You need only to call.

The psalm ends with ‘every creature’. Your praise joins a song as wide as creation.
